references.text: In [ref:Joh 20:20|John 20:20], Jesus shows his disciples his hands and his side after the resurrection, a parallel account where the physical evidence of the crucifixion confirms his identity and resurrection.

In [ref:Joh 20:25-27|John 20:25-27], Thomas refuses to believe without seeing the nail marks, and Jesus invites him to put his fingers into the nail marks and his hand into Jesus' side. This underscores the same point—the physical wounds as proof of the resurrection.

The immediate context in [ref:Luk 24:36-39|Luke 24:36-39] shows that the disciples were startled and thought they saw a spirit, so Jesus invited them to look at and touch his hands and feet to confirm that he had flesh and bones. Verse 40 is the direct action following this invitation.
[ref:Sal 22:17|Psalm 22:17] is a prophetic text speaking of hands and feet being pierced—a messianic prophecy pointing forward to the crucifixion and the wounds Jesus now displays as proof.
[ref:Sak 13:6|Zechariah 13:6] speaks of wounds on the body, which in Christian tradition are linked to the Messiah's suffering and the marks that Jesus bears after the crucifixion.
In [ref:Jes 49:16|Isaiah 49:16], the Lord says he has engraved his people on the palms of his hands. The image of marks on the hands can be read as a foreshadowing reference to Christ's nail wounds.

In [ref:Apg 1:3|Acts 1:3], Luke writes that after his suffering, Jesus "presented himself alive to them by many proofs" over forty days. Showing his hands and feet is precisely such convincing proof of the bodily resurrection.

[ref:1 Joh 1:1|1 John 1:1] testifies that the apostles had seen with their eyes and touched with their hands what concerns the Word of life—a possible reference to just such encounters where the risen Jesus allowed himself to be physically touched.
